query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high‐entropy alloys, brittle behavior during service at intermediate temperatures emerges from shear‐driven dynamic grain refinement that produces an ultrafine, high‐angle grain boundary network. This network, rather than classical impurity segregation or grain-boundary precipitation, becomes unstable under tensile loading, leading to decohesion at the grain boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a relatively coarse-grained, chemically homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply high strain rates at intermediate temperatures (approximately 400–800°C) under controlled, inert or ultra-high vacuum conditions to avoid extrinsic effects such as oxidation or impurity segregation.
generation.conditions: Intermediate service temperatures (400–800°C) and high loading rates where dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement can be activated without significant thermal impurity segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-refined nanocrystalline grain boundary network (grain sizes approaching 10–50 nm) that possesses high-angle, high-energy boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under high strain rate deformation at intermediate temperatures, extensive shear induces dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement. As the grain size drops below a critical threshold, the mechanism of plastic deformation shifts from dislocation-mediated slip to grain boundary sliding. The high energy and reduced cohesive strength of these refined grain boundaries lead to intergranular debonding (decohesion) during tensile loading, resulting in premature failure and brittle behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the coarse-grained baseline state, the dynamically refined alloy will show a marked reduction in ductility and toughness, with fracture surfaces exhibiting intergranular decohesion and reduced strain hardening. The onset of brittle failure will occur earlier despite the alloy’s inherent high strength.
generation.baseline: The same high-entropy alloy in its initial coarse-grained, homogeneous state exhibits favorable toughness and ductility, with deformation primarily via dislocation slip rather than grain boundary sliding.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under intermediate temperature and high strain rate conditions. At lower temperatures, dynamic grain refinement might be suppressed, and at higher temperatures, thermally activated processes (such as diffusion-driven boundary relaxation) might mitigate the decohesion tendency.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical grain size at which the transition to brittle decohesion occurs and the influence of minor compositional variations on the threshold remain to be quantified. There is also uncertainty regarding the interplay between dynamic grain boundary strengthening and weakening during service.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the single-phase high-entropy alloy with an initially coarse microstructure. Subject these samples to high-strain-rate deformation at intermediate temperatures (400–800°C) under ultra-high vacuum conditions. Utilize in-situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to monitor grain size evolution and post-deformation fractographic analysis (e.g., scanning electron microscopy) to assess fracture mode.
measurements: Grain size distribution before and after deformation (to detect refinement to ~10–50 nm scale)
Fracture surface morphology (to identify intergranular decohesion versus transgranular failure)
Stress–strain curves capturing onset of brittle behavior (loss of ductility and strain hardening)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If deformation under the specified conditions does not produce significant nanocrystalline grain refinement, or if the fracture surfaces show predominantly transgranular features with no evidence of intergranular decohesion, then the hypothesis that brittle behavior is mediated by dynamic grain boundary decohesion is falsified.

Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
